questions.stem: A student counts oxygen bubbles from pondweed at different distances from a lamp. As the lamp moves closer, more bubbles are produced. What relationship does this demonstrate?

options.text: Temperature increases the rate of photosynthesis
Increasing light intensity increases the rate of photosynthesis
CO2 concentration increases with light
The pondweed is respiring faster

questions.explanation: Moving the lamp closer increases the light intensity reaching the plant (light intensity is inversely proportional to distance squared). More light energy means faster photosynthesis, producing more oxygen. This is a standard required practical for measuring the rate of photosynthesis.

questions.stem: In the pondweed experiment, a student uses a heat shield (glass screen of water) between the lamp and the plant. Why?

options.text: To filter out the light so only some reaches the plant
To absorb heat from the lamp so that temperature does not become a confounding variable
To magnify the light and increase its intensity
To prevent the water from evaporating

questions.explanation: The lamp produces both light and heat. If the heat warms the water around the pondweed, the temperature would increase as the lamp moves closer, making it impossible to determine whether changes in bubble rate are due to light or temperature. The glass water screen absorbs infrared radiation (heat) while allowing visible light through, keeping temperature constant.

questions.stem: A graph shows that increasing temperature from 10 to 30 degrees C increases the rate of photosynthesis, but above 40 degrees C the rate drops sharply. What explains the drop?

options.text: The plant stops absorbing light at high temperatures
Enzymes involved in photosynthesis become denatured above their optimum temperature
CO2 becomes less soluble in warm water
Chlorophyll breaks down at high temperatures

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis involves enzyme-controlled reactions. Above the optimum temperature, enzymes begin to denature -- their active sites change shape and they can no longer catalyse the reactions. This causes a rapid decrease in the rate of photosynthesis. Between 10-30 degrees C, increasing temperature increases kinetic energy and reaction rate.

questions.stem: Instead of counting bubbles, a student collects the gas produced by pondweed in a syringe over 5 minutes. Why is measuring gas volume more accurate than counting bubbles?

options.text: Syringes are easier to use than counting
Bubbles may vary in size, so counting them does not give a reliable measure of the actual volume of gas produced
Gas volume is always the same regardless of conditions
Counting bubbles gives a higher value than actual gas production

questions.explanation: Bubbles can vary considerably in size -- a few large bubbles could contain more gas than many small ones. Counting bubbles therefore gives an unreliable estimate of the total oxygen produced. Collecting gas in a syringe or measuring cylinder gives a direct, accurate measurement of volume, making the data more reliable and valid.

questions.stem: Adding sodium hydrogencarbonate (NaHCO3) to the water around pondweed increases the rate of bubble production. What does NaHCO3 provide?

options.text: Extra oxygen for the plant
Extra carbon dioxide (as a source of dissolved CO2) for photosynthesis
Nutrients for the plant to grow
An alkaline environment that increases enzyme activity

questions.explanation: Sodium hydrogencarbonate dissolves in water to release CO2, which is a raw material for photosynthesis. By increasing the CO2 available to the pondweed, the rate of photosynthesis increases (assuming CO2 was the limiting factor). This is a common way to vary CO2 concentration in the pondweed experiment.
